description: Around an Athenian dinner, the guests take turns defining love. Aristophanes tells the story of the androgynes, Socrates lifts desire toward the Beautiful. Plato turns a party into philosophy.

hero.hook: An evening with far too much wine. And suddenly, the finest definition of love ever written.

blocks.text: In Athens, in the **4th century BC**, **Plato**, the Greek philosopher and student of Socrates, wrote the **Symposium**. The Greek title is *Symposion*. The setting is an [[Athenian symposion]], the men's gathering after dinner where watered wine and intellectual talk went together. That evening the set theme is **[[Eros]]**, the force that drives the soul toward beauty.

Each guest offers a theory of love. The dialogue becomes a climb: from the body to beauty, from beauty to the **Forms**, the perfect and eternal patterns Plato believed in. And **Socrates**, Plato's teacher, sentenced to death in 399, has the last word, as he so often does in Plato's dialogues.

The party celebrates a prize won by the poet **Agathon**, a tragic playwright and the host of the evening. The hangovers from the night before are still there, so the guests decide to praise Eros instead of drinking too much. The speeches follow one another: doctors, poets, politicians. Each man projects his own view of desire. **Phaedrus** presents love as the engine of courage. **Pausanias** separates noble love from coarse love.

blocks.caption: The Greek symposion: wine, garlands and talk as a social sport

blocks.text: Plato uses the party to do philosophy without a lecture. People laugh, provoke each other, correct each other. The argument moves along with the wine, but also thanks to the rule of the game: each man has to defend Eros in front of the others. The contest of eloquence, the Greek *agon*, becomes a school of thought.

The most famous speech belongs to **Aristophanes**, the Athenian comic playwright known for his satires. Long ago, he says, human beings were double. The [[androgynes]] carried both male and female features. Other pairs were joined in the same way. **Zeus**, king of the gods, cut them in two as a punishment. Ever since, each of us has been looking for the lost half.
This story is where the word “soulmate” comes from. Plato puts it in the mouth of a comic playwright, then moves past it: love does not stop at finding a lost body.

The myth is lovely, tender, a little sad. It explains **lack**, the sense of being incomplete that pushes us toward someone else. But Socrates goes somewhere else: loving is not just gluing two halves together. It is climbing toward something larger than yourself.

Socrates reports the teaching of **Diotima**, a foreign priestess and the voice of wisdom in the dialogue. Eros is neither a full god nor a poor mortal: he is a [[daimon]], a being halfway between gods and men. He desires what he lacks. The lover starts from a beautiful body, moves on to beautiful souls, then to beautiful actions, and reaches **Beauty itself**, the perfect Form of beauty.

blocks.caption: Socrates and Alcibiades: desire can also be a school for the soul

blocks.text: This is [[Platonic Eros]], a desire that educates. Later [[Alcibiades]], a young Athenian politician, handsome and unstable, bursts in drunk and praises Socrates as a disturbing satyr. Philosophical love does not abolish physical trouble. It turns that trouble into a search for truth.

sections.title: Diotima and the ladder of love

blocks.text: In everyday speech, a “platonic” love means one without sex. In Plato it is richer than that: the body is a starting point, not a shame. The Symposium shaped Christian theology, the love poetry of Petrarch and Ronsard, and the psychology of desire. It shows that loving also means learning how to see.
In the **Symposium**, Plato turns one Athenian evening into a ladder: you start from physical desire and aim at a wider beauty. Loving, here, means learning to see further than yourself.
